cf.title: ANSI SQL proposal: SELECT DISTINCT ON (... ORDER BY ...) and UNION DISTINCT ON (... ORDER BY ...)

input.subject: ANSI SQL proposal: SELECT DISTINCT ON (... ORDER BY ...) and UNION DISTINCT ON (... ORDER BY ...)

verdict_reasoning: Level 1b fails on two fixable objections. standards-compat-1: message #9 says wider approval of the syntax comes only after v19, and message #4 endorses only the inline ORDER BY, so the UNION form would ship ahead of the committee. demand-1: the thread shows no non-recursive workload that DISTINCT ON over a UNION ALL subquery does not already serve. The inline ORDER BY for SELECT drew no surviving objection.

brief.title: Inline ORDER BY in DISTINCT ON, and UNION DISTINCT ON with recursive pruning
brief.problem: DISTINCT ON requires its keys to lead the query's ORDER BY, so picking the kept row and sorting the output cannot be done separately without a subquery. There is no way to deduplicate on a subset of columns during a UNION. In WITH RECURSIVE, UNION ALL with CYCLE explores every path, so shortest-path queries grow combinatorially.
brief.proposed_design: DISTINCT ON takes an optional ORDER BY inside its parentheses that picks the row kept per key, separate from the outer ORDER BY. UNION gains DISTINCT ON (keys [ORDER BY ...]), planned as HashAggregate or Sort plus Unique. In WITH RECURSIVE, a better row replaces the stored entry and goes back into the work table, so the recursion keeps the best row per key until convergence.
user_visible_surface: New syntax: select distinct on (keys order by sort_keys) ..., with the outer ORDER BY no longer required to match the keys.
New syntax: select ... union distinct on (keys [order by sort_keys]) select ..., also for nested and multi-way set operations.
WITH RECURSIVE with UNION DISTINCT ON (... ORDER BY ...) prunes rows per key; SEARCH and CYCLE are rejected with an inline ORDER BY.
EXPLAIN shows a "Sort Key:" line for HashAggregate and RecursiveUnion when tie-break sort columns are used.
author_claims: The inline ORDER BY separates the choice of kept row from the output order, so no subquery is needed.
Recursive UNION DISTINCT ON allows shortest-path and Bellman-Ford style search in plain SQL without infinite loops.
The syntax follows the SQL precedent of ORDER BY inside OVER, WITHIN GROUP and aggregate calls.
The author drafted a SQL standard discussion paper and plans to seek wider approval of the syntax after the v19 release.
The author says the design looks similar to DuckDB's USING KEY.
brief.thread_state: Vik Fearing supports the inline ORDER BY but asked for a UNION DISTINCT ON use case, which Hannu gave as a recursive shortest-path query. Manu reported no wrong results in about 42,000 cases, an 820x recursive speedup and a planner fix for group estimates, which v3 does not include yet.
unclear: Whether the SQL committee has seen or accepted the syntax; extending non-standard DISTINCT ON first risks a later conflict with the standard.
The recursive mode loops until statement_timeout on negative cycles; the proposal does not say whether that is accepted or documented.
Whether pruning ties results to the order rows arrive in, and how that matches standard WITH RECURSIVE semantics.
Why SEARCH and CYCLE are rejected with an inline ORDER BY, and whether the docs say so.
Only Vik Fearing and Manu replied; no committer has commented on the planner and executor changes.
Patch 0005 fixes bugs in 0001-0004, so the series layout for commit is not settled.

prior_attempts.title: Removing useless DISTINCT clauses
prior_attempts.quote: Once I noticed that, I became convinced that this patch actually breaks planning of sort/unique-based DISTINCT: if we have a pkey a,b, but the ORDER BY list is a,c,b, then we will sort by a,c,b but the Unique node will be told it only needs to unique-ify on the first two sort columns.
prior_attempts.reason: Tom Lane found that removing distinctClause items breaks the parser-enforced match between DISTINCT and ORDER BY, which create_distinct_paths relies on. With a primary key on (a,b), `select distinct * from t1 order by a,c,b` hits an assertion and crashes the server. He judged the fix too large for the last day of the commitfest.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P2 removed DISTINCT columns inside the planner; this proposal lets the user separate DISTINCT ON keys from the outer ORDER BY. Both relax the parser-enforced match between DISTINCT and ORDER BY.

objections.title: New DISTINCT ON spellings ship before the standard committee has reviewed them
objections.failure_scenario: Postgres ships `union distinct on (k order by c)` in a release, and users put it in views. The committee later adopts a different spelling or different tie-break rules for subset deduplication. Postgres must then support both forms indefinitely, and portable SQL using the standard form behaves differently from existing Postgres views.
objections.argument: The discussion paper (message #1) is a draft, and message #9 says wider approval will be sought only after v19. The standard already covers per-key selection with QUALIFY and FETCH FIRST ... PARTITIONS BY (message #4), and DuckDB uses USING KEY for the recursive case (message #6), so the committee has other spellings to choose from. Vik Fearing endorsed the inline ORDER BY for SELECT but questioned UNION DISTINCT ON, and that is the part with no precedent at all.
objections.author_must_show: Has WG 3 seen the UNION DISTINCT ON form, and would the Postgres design still hold if the committee chose USING KEY or different semantics?

critic.reasoning: Message #9 confirms that wider approval of the syntax comes only after v19, and message #4 endorses only the inline ORDER BY. Postgres already carries non-standard DISTINCT ON, but that does not answer the risk for the new UNION form.

objections.title: Non-recursive UNION DISTINCT ON has no use case beyond a workaround
objections.failure_scenario: A user who wants the newest row per key across two tables writes DISTINCT ON over a UNION ALL subquery today, and it works. With the patch the project carries new set-operation grammar, Append-flattening guards and pushdown checks for that case. No user story shows the subquery form failing.
objections.argument: In message #4 Vik Fearing asked for a UNION DISTINCT ON use case, and message #5 gave only a recursive shortest-path query. In message #8 the non-recursive form was 1.36x slower than the classic rewrite at 200k groups. Message #10 shows a gain only with an unmerged estimate diff, and a loss again at 500k groups. The discussion paper argues for early pruning but gives no workload where the rewrite is too slow.
objections.author_must_show: Which real non-recursive queries need UNION DISTINCT ON, and why is DISTINCT ON over a UNION ALL subquery not enough for them?

critic.reasoning: The discussion paper gives a non-recursive example (active and archived users), but DISTINCT ON over a UNION ALL subquery does that job today. Messages #8 and #10 show no consistent gain over that rewrite, and the thread names no workload that needs the new form.

other_surviving.title: Recursive UNION DISTINCT ON departs from WITH RECURSIVE semantics without documenting it
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A user writes a shortest-path query over a graph with a negative-cost cycle, or adds the standard CYCLE clause for safety. The first query runs until statement_timeout and the second fails with an error. The user learns about either limit only at run time, because the docs do not mention them.
other_surviving.argument: Standard WITH RECURSIVE only accumulates rows. In this mode a later row replaces a stored one and goes back into the work table (0004 commit message), so the query may never reach a fixpoint. Message #10 shows that negative cycles never terminate. 0005 rejects SEARCH and CYCLE with an inline ORDER BY, but the select.sgml hunks state neither restriction, and so users cannot rely on CYCLE as their usual guard against runaway recursion.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Will the documentation define the recursive mode as replacement rather than accumulation, list the SEARCH/CYCLE restriction and the non-termination case, and say why CYCLE cannot be supported?

critic.reasoning: Message #10 confirms that a negative cycle runs until statement_timeout, and 0005 rejects SEARCH and CYCLE with an inline ORDER BY. The select.sgml hunks shown state neither limit, and the proposal gives no reason for the restriction.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: No committer engaged; the five-patch series is all-or-nothing
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A committer pushes 0001-0004 for review, but 0005 carries memory-safety and wrong-result fixes for them. Bugs in hashed DISTINCT ON or RecursiveUnion are then reported after release, and nobody who knows the new paths is on the thread to fix them.
other_surviving.argument: The series touches about 30 files across parser, planner, executor, ruleutils and rewriteSearchCycle. Message #8 shows 0001-0004 alone crash under ASan and give wrong results, so no prefix of the series can be committed safely. Only Vik Fearing, on syntax, and Manu, on testing, replied. No committer has engaged with the planner or executor changes.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Can the series be reordered so that 0001 plus the inline DISTINCT ON patch stand alone, each correct without 0005?

critic.reasoning: Message #8 shows 0001-0004 without 0005 crash and return wrong results, so no prefix of the series stands alone; this is a design-level concern about the series shape. The missing committer is a committability note and must not raise the verdict.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: Relaxing the DISTINCT ON and ORDER BY match drops a planner invariant
refuted.failure_scenario: A user writes select distinct on (a order by b) ... order by c. A planner path or extension still assumes the distinct keys lead the sort keys, so it sorts by c and unique-ifies on a prefix. The user gets wrong rows or an assertion failure, and only on the plan shapes that reach that path.
refuted.argument: Today the parser forces DISTINCT ON keys to lead ORDER BY, and [P2] shows planner code relying on that match. Its failure mode was a Unique node fed rows sorted on the wrong columns. Message #8 found Assert(numCols <= pathkeys) and wrong results with 0001-0004, which 0005 fixed. That shows the invariant is in use, but the proposal does not list every place that relied on it or say why each one still holds.
refuted.author_must_show: Which planner and executor paths assumed distinct keys lead the sort keys, and how does each now handle an inline ORDER BY?

critic.reasoning: The objection names no path that still assumes the match. 0005 fixes the needed_pathkeys prefix check, and message #8 reports 0 divergences in about 42,000 cases on the full series, including the MergeAppend plus Unique paths.

refuted.title: Recursive UNION DISTINCT ON never terminates on negative cycles
refuted.failure_scenario: A user runs a shortest-path query over a finite graph that contains a negative-cost cycle. Plain UNION would stop once no new rows appear. This query keeps finding better rows until statement_timeout, and the user may never learn why.
refuted.argument: Message #10 reports that a negative cycle has no fixpoint and runs until statement_timeout. The doc hunk in 0004 presents the feature as a way to find optimal paths and does not state this limit. Plain UNION over a finite domain terminates, so users may expect the same here. [P4] is weak support only: its AI summary records doubt that a new recursive loop terminates.
refuted.author_must_show: Will the docs state the non-termination case, or will the executor detect a non-converging key and raise an error?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2, which covers the negative-cycle case together with the SEARCH and CYCLE restriction. [P4] concerns a parse-tree rewrite and must not be used as support.

refuted.title: Recursive pruning adds a second RecursiveUnion mode with open termination
refuted.failure_scenario: A user writes a cost search over a graph that has a negative cycle, and the query runs until statement_timeout with no error. Later, a developer changes rewriteSearchCycle or nodeRecursiveunion.c for an unrelated WITH RECURSIVE feature and does not handle the replace-and-requeue mode. Nothing fails until a user reports wrong results.
refuted.argument: Patch 0004 makes RecursiveUnion replace stored rows and send them back into the work table, which changes its fixpoint behaviour. Message #10 confirms that negative cycles never finish, and the docs hunk does not mention this. Patch 0005 rejects SEARCH and CYCLE with an inline ORDER BY and gives no reason. [P4] stalled on the same two points: changes to rewriteSearchAndCycle() and a loop that was not shown to terminate.
refuted.author_must_show: What termination guarantee does the recursive mode give, how is non-termination documented, and why can SEARCH and CYCLE not be combined with it?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2 on termination and on SEARCH and CYCLE. The remaining part, that a later developer forgets the new mode, names no concrete path and would apply to any new executor mode.

refuted.title: UNION DISTINCT ON fixes non-standard syntax before the committee sees it
refuted.failure_scenario: Postgres ships UNION DISTINCT ON in a release. The SQL committee later adopts a keyed set operation with different spelling or recursive semantics. Postgres then has to keep its form forever next to the standard one, and users must learn which one they wrote.
refuted.argument: Message #9 says wider approval of the syntax will be sought only after v19, so committing it first sets Postgres behaviour in stone. Message #4 notes that the standard already covers per-key selection with QUALIFY and FETCH FIRST ... PARTITIONS BY. Message #4 supports only the inline ORDER BY and asks for the UNION use case. Message #6 points to a related design, USING KEY in DuckDB, which shows the design space is not settled.
refuted.author_must_show: Why should UNION DISTINCT ON and its recursive mode go in before the committee responds, instead of shipping only the inline ORDER BY first?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which states the same risk with the same thread references and a more concrete failure scenario.

refuted.title: Recursive pruning demand rests on one puzzle and one paper
refuted.failure_scenario: The project adds replace-and-requeue semantics to RecursiveUnion for shortest-path search. If only puzzle solvers and graph experiments use it, every later change to nodeRecursiveunion.c and rewriteSearchCycle.c must preserve a mode that few people run. Breakage then surfaces only from rare bug reports.
refuted.argument: The demand shown is an Advent of Code example in message #5 and a DuckDB paper found two days before message #6. The 820x speedup in message #8 is real but measured on synthetic graphs. Nobody in the thread reports a production graph or routing workload that hit this wall, and only two people replied. The DuckDB precedent counts as some evidence, but it does not show how many users need it.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users run shortest-path or state-space queries in Postgres today, and what do they use now: pgRouting, application code, or UNION ALL with CYCLE?

critic.reasoning: Message #8 shows the existing SQL form cannot do the job: UNION ALL with CYCLE no longer finishes within 2 GB of temp space from a 6x6 grid up. DuckDB's USING KEY, cited in message #6, shows another system added this capability.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The series adds fields to parse, path and plan nodes and a new ReplaceTupleHashEntryIfBetter() in executor.h.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: It adds DISTINCT ON (keys ORDER BY ...) and UNION DISTINCT ON, both non-standard, with only a draft discussion paper behind them.

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: It adds HashAggregate and MergeAppend plus Unique paths for DISTINCT ON and changes set-operation grouping and qual pushdown.

touch_points.label: pg_dump / restore round-trip
touch_points.reason: Views can contain both new forms, so dump and restore depend on the new pg_get_viewdef() deparsing in ruleutils.c.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-1: New DISTINCT ON spellings ship before the standard committee has reviewed them

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: RecursiveUnion gains a replace-and-requeue mode, and about 30 files change across parser, planner, executor and rewriter.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The series changes execGrouping.c and nodeAgg.c, which every hashed aggregate uses; message #8 reports no measurable regression.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: Non-recursive UNION DISTINCT ON can be written today as DISTINCT ON over a UNION ALL subquery.

questions: Has WG 3 seen the UNION DISTINCT ON form, and would the Postgres design still hold if the committee chose USING KEY or different semantics?
Which real non-recursive queries need UNION DISTINCT ON, and why is DISTINCT ON over a UNION ALL subquery not enough for them?
Can the series be reordered so that 0001 plus the inline ORDER BY patch stand alone, each correct without 0005?
Will the docs define the recursive mode as replacement, state the negative-cycle case, and explain why SEARCH and CYCLE are rejected with an inline ORDER BY?
Does the result of recursive pruning depend on the order in which rows arrive, and if so, in which cases?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows set-operation planning, hashed aggregation and nodeRecursiveunion.c. Only Vik Fearing, on syntax, and Manu, on testing, have replied.
committability.liability: The owner signs for two new syntax forms that cannot be removed once views use them, and for a second RecursiveUnion mode that every later WITH RECURSIVE change must preserve.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted a rebase and a v3 with a fix patch in message #7, and answered the use-case question in message #5.

priority.reason: The inline ORDER BY answers a common pattern and has support in message #4, but the series ties it to UNION DISTINCT ON and the recursive mode. Those two parts carry the open syntax and demand questions, and the series spans about 30 files.

provisional_note: Two level 2 objections survived but were not evaluated: the undocumented recursive limits (standards-compat-2) and the series shape (maintenance-fit-2). The security_barrier pushdown rule and the full set of planner paths that relied on the DISTINCT ON and ORDER BY match cannot be judged without the code.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: parallel distinct union and aggregate support patch
precedents_retrieved.objectors: David Steele, David Rowley, Daniel Gustafsson
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a Parallel BatchSort node, and later a batch HashAggregate, that hash-partitions tuples into shared batches so each parallel worker sorts or aggregates whole batches for distinct, union and aggregate. A later version replaced this with an unbuffered Parallel Redistribute node that sends tuples to workers through shared memory queues, spilling to a SharedTuplestore.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry was returned with feedback because the patch needed a rebase for many months and the thread stalled. It got no review for two commitfests, and David Steele and David Rowley said the author had not answered reviewers who suggested an unbuffered Parallel Partition style operator. The author posted a Redistribute version in September 2021, but the visible messages show no review of it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Many months on and this patch still needs a rebase to apply, and the thread has
stalled.  I'm marking this Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Removing useless DISTINCT clauses
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch applies the existing GROUP BY optimization to plain DISTINCT. When a table's primary key columns are all in the DISTINCT clause, the planner drops the other columns of that table from the distinctClause.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane found that removing distinctClause items breaks the parser-enforced match between DISTINCT and ORDER BY, which create_distinct_paths relies on. With a primary key on (a,b), `select distinct * from t1 order by a,c,b` hits an assertion and crashes the server. He judged the fix too large for the last day of the commitfest.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Once I noticed that, I became convinced that this patch actually
breaks planning of sort/unique-based DISTINCT: if we have a pkey a,b,
but the ORDER BY list is a,c,b, then we will sort by a,c,b but the
Unique node will be told it only needs to unique-ify on the first two
sort columns.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove useless distinct clauses
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes the planner drop a DISTINCT clause when the selected columns include the primary key of a table, and turns inner joins to other tables into semi-joins. When the query has no ORDER BY, it uses the DISTINCT columns as the sort clause.
precedents_retrieved.objection: David Rowley found that the patch returns wrong results: with cross joins, select distinct a from t cross join pg_class cross join pg_attribute returns many rows where it should return one, because the change from inner joins to semi-joins is broken. He also objected that the patch clears parse->distinctClause directly, has no comments on why each transformation is valid, and does not follow the source format. The author did not answer the review, so Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Also, the processing of the join tree where you switch inner joins to
semi joins looks broken.  This would require much more careful and
recursive processing to do properly.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow multiple recursive self-references
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the recursive term of a `with recursive` query reference the CTE more than once, with all references reading the same working table, while still allowing only linear recursion. It also rotates the UNION parse tree in parse analysis so that non-recursive and recursive branches can appear in any order.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane's review found that the patch appears to break rewriteSearchAndCycle(), which assumes a recursive query is a UNION of exactly two SELECTs. He also found the tree-rotation and checkWellFormedSelectStmt changes undercommented and was not convinced the new loop terminates. Peter Eisentraut accepted the semantics and executor changes but still disputed the parse-analysis rewrite and would not commit without another reviewer. No author reply follows Tom Lane's review, and the entry was closed after waiting on the author.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Doesn't it break rewriteSearchAndCycle() completely?  That code assumes (without a lot of checking) that a recursive query is a UNION [ALL] of exactly two SELECTs.

precedents_retrieved.title: ALTER TABLE: emit NOTICE when ONLY is omitted but no partition recursion occurs
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes ALTER TABLE on a partitioned table, run without ONLY, emit a NOTICE when the sub-command does not recurse to partitions. It started with REPLICA IDENTITY and in v4 covered other sub-commands such as SET SCHEMA, OWNER TO, SET TABLESPACE and row level security.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Reviewers changed the message level from WARNING to NOTICE and changed its wording, and Jim Jones called the v4 code fine apart from the hint style. The thread ends with Jim Jones planning more tests, and no message explains the withdrawal.

precedents_retrieved.title: Union Replacement of OR logic
precedents_retrieved.summary: The entry title names a replacement of OR logic with UNION, but the shown messages belong to a different thread, "brininsert optimization opportunity". That thread proposes keeping the BRIN revmap access struct across inserts and cleaning it up through a new aminsertcleanup callback, and the shown messages do not describe the OR proposal.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The shown thread ends with Tomas Vondra pushing the brininsert fix patches, and none of the messages discuss the OR-to-UNION proposal or its rejection.

precedents_retrieved.title: allow partial union-all and improve parallel subquery costing
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the planner build partial paths for UNION ALL so the branches can run under a parallel plan. It also changes subquery costing to account for parallelism, with a regression test and before/after plans for TPC-DS query 5.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No reviewer took up the patch during the commitfests. In March 2021 the patch no longer applied, and the entry was set to Waiting for Author. The author sent no rebased patch, so the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Since no new patch has been provided, marking this Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add support for Distinct in Window aggregates
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add support for Distinct in Window aggregates

precedents_retrieved.title: [PoC] Implementation of distinct in Window Aggregates: take two
precedents_retrieved.summary: The PoC patch adds DISTINCT support to window aggregates, for single-column aggregates without ORDER BY, by mirroring the nodeAgg approach. Each partition's input values go into a tuplesort, which is sorted and deduplicated in finalize_windowaggregate before the transition function runs.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch crashed in cfbot and failed the regress, postgres_fdw, recovery and pg_upgrade tests. The author did not reply to that report, so the CommitFest manager moved the entry to Returned with Feedback. No one objected to the design.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
Reverted commit(s): Optimize order of GROUP BY keys
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit db0d67db2401eb6238ccc04c6407a4fd4f985832 and
several follow-on fixes.  The idea of making a cost-based choice
of the order of the sorting columns is not fundamentally unsound,
but it requires cost information and data statistics that we don't
really have.  For example, relying on procost to distinguish the
relative costs of different sort comparators is pretty pointless
so long as most such comparator functions are labeled with cost 1.0.
Moreover, estimating the number of comparisons done by Quicksort
requires more than just an estimate of the number of distinct values
in the input: you also need some idea of the sizes of the larger
groups, if you want an estimate that's good to better than a factor of
three or so.  That's data that's often unknown or not very reliable.
Worse, to arrive at estimates of the number of calls made to the
lower-order-column comparison functions, the code needs to make
estimates of the numbers of distinct values of multiple columns,
which are necessarily even less trustworthy than per-column stats.
Even if all the inputs are perfectly reliable, the cost algorithm
as-implemented cannot offer useful information about how to order
sorting columns beyond the point at which the average group size
is estimated to drop to 1.

Close inspection of the code added by db0d67db2 shows that there
are also multiple small bugs.  These could have been fixed, but
there's not much point if we don't trust the estimates to be
accurate in-principle.

Finally, the changes in cost_sort's behavior made for very large
changes (often a factor of 2 or so) in the cost estimates for all
sorting operations, not only those for multi-column GROUP BY.
That naturally changes plan choices in many situations, and there's
precious little evidence to show that the changes are for the better.
Given the above doubts about whether the new estimates are really
trustworthy, it's hard to summon much confidence that these changes
are better on the average.

Since we're hard up against the release deadline for v15, let's
revert these changes for now.  We can always try again later.

Note: in v15, I left T_PathKeyInfo in place in nodes.h even though
it's unreferenced.  Removing it would be an ABI break, and it seems
a bit late in the release cycle for that.

logic substantially, by introducing a third code path that required
different behavior in the function's main loop.  That seems quite
unnecessary on closer inspection: the new IsBinaryUpgrade case can
just share the behavior of the other immediate-unlink cases.  Hence,
revert 4ab5dae94 and most of 0e758ae89 (keeping the latter's
save/restore errno fix), and add IsBinaryUpgrade to the set of
conditions tested to choose immediate unlink.

Also fix some additional places with sloppy handling of errno,
to ensure we have an invariant that we always continue processing
after any non-ENOENT failure of do_truncate.  I doubt that that's
fixing any bug of field importance, so I don't feel it necessary to
back-patch; but we might as well get it right while we're here.

Also improve the comments, which had drifted a bit from what the
code actually does, and neglected to mention some important
considerations.

Back-patch to v15, not because this is fixing any bug but because
it doesn't seem like a good idea for v15's mdunlinkfork logic to be
significantly different from both v14 and v16.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent proposed the same idea. The two related rows match risks this patch takes on, so both are raised above.

Two objections raised. No backward-compatibility break was found for existing DISTINCT ON queries. New syntax failing to load into an older server is normal for any new syntax and is not counted as an objection.

The proposal changes no on-disk format, WAL record, replication path or wire protocol message. New parse-node and plan-node fields land in stored view rules and in plans sent to parallel workers, but a major release with a catversion bump already covers that. pg_upgrade rebuilds views from SQL, and the patch adds pg_get_viewdef() deparsing for both new forms. Changes to executor and planner structs affect extensions only at a major release, as usual.

The proposal adds query syntax and executor strategies with no new privilege or exposure, so the security angle finds no design-level objection. Any user can already write a WITH RECURSIVE query that runs until statement_timeout, so the negative-cycle loop adds no new denial of service. Comparators and user operators run as in existing DISTINCT ON sorts. The 'security issues' that 0005 fixes are memory-safety bugs in the code, which is out of scope here. The pushdown rule for security_barrier views over UNION DISTINCT ON cannot be checked without the code.
Hot-path cost was not raised as an objection: message #8 found no measurable regression for untouched features, and the hashing cost falls on users of the new syntax.

Each existing alternative is either a convenience gap or cannot do the job. The inline ORDER BY replaces one subquery around classic DISTINCT ON, and Vik Fearing endorsed it in message #4. Non-recursive UNION DISTINCT ON can be written today as DISTINCT ON over a UNION ALL subquery. But it shares syntax and machinery with the recursive form, so dropping it saves little. Recursive per-key pruning has no equivalent today: UNION compares whole rows and UNION ALL with CYCLE explores every path (message #8). No extension or hook offers it outside core.
The inline ORDER BY in SELECT DISTINCT ON has support from Vik Fearing in message #4 and answers a common pattern, so no demand objection is raised against that part.
